title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 17: A Plea for Honesty
keywords: National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP)
a change of men, not a change in men
primary_topics: Chapter 17 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's keynote address of November 17, 1988 to the National Student Congress of the NUSP in Cebu City, delivered 30 years after he founded the union as a young Far Eastern University student leader.

A retrospective on the NUSP: born 'as a rebellion against a decadent student milieu' muzzled by the government, founded on the proposition that the best in man and society is attained 'only in freedom, dignity, equality and responsibility,' and now grown beyond student concerns into the nation's battles.

His central question to the young: why, among the peoples of the Pacific, the Philippines alone has remained poor -- ruling out dictatorship, foreign exploitation, poor education and professional inferiority as the explanation.

His answer and his plea: the 'godfather mentality' and 'dole-out syndrome' have made LUSOT, LAKAS and LAGAY -- chicanery, influence and bribery -- substitutes for honest work, and since 1986 brought 'a change of leaders, not a change in values,' he challenges the NUSP to lead a crusade for honesty, hard work and self-discipline.
sub_topics: He thanks NUSP president Lorenzo Tanada III and recalls his own student days 30 years earlier -- his 'search for identity,' 'singleminded pursuit of excellence' and 'formation of enduring values' -- when 'I was very poor; I had nothing' and therefore was truly free.

He recounts his record: elected FEU Central Student Organization president as a second-year law student in 1957, then organizing and heading the NUSP through 1960, and from 1960 to 1962 founding the Institute of Student Affairs, later World University Service, Philippines.

He names the generations of NUSP leaders -- Emanuel Soriano, Fernando Lagua, Alfonso Aguirre, Homobono Adaza and others in the late '50s; Raul Roco, Rene Saguisag and others in the early '60s; and an alumni roll through the '80s including Miriam Defensor-Santiago, Jose Cuisia, Edgar Jopson, Francis Pangilinan, Lean Alejandro and Chito Gascon.

He restates the union's founding ideals: that the young must be freed 'from the political apron strings of the old,' that the student can think for himself, and that freedom, dignity, equality and responsibility are the conditions of excellence.

He congratulates the union -- 'Well done! Well done!' -- for accomplishing more than its founders dreamt, moving from purely secular student concerns to the battles against corruption, dictatorship, imperialism and terrorism, and now against poverty, colonialism, oppression and decadence.

He frames the address as a vision for the next 30 years rather than a congratulation for the last, granting that the dictatorship has fallen and Congress been restored, but insisting 'this does not mean that our problems are over.'

He poses the question -- why are the Philippines and the Filipinos the only ones in the Pacific who have remained poor? -- and disposes of four explanations: dictators (Korea, Taiwan and Singapore had them too, 'without meaning to mitigate the guilt of the man in Hawaii'), foreign exploitation, inferior education, and professional inferiority, since the Filipino 'always excels' abroad and 'is praised everywhere, except when he is in his own country.'

He offers his own explanation: the Filipino has spoiled himself into believing he can do nothing alone and must depend on a patron -- the 'godfather mentality' that reaches for a recommendation instead of qualifications, for the judge instead of the merits, and failing that for chicanery and then bribery.

He renders the malaise in Tagalog as the three 'L's -- LAKAS (influence), LUSOT (chicanery) and LAGAY (bribery) -- illustrated by his favorite taxi driver, who sweet-talks, then drops the police chief's name, then produces a 20-peso bill, and 'merrily gets away' to mess up traffic again.

He blames culture and government systems, and particularly '20 years of Marcosian dictatorship,' for training people to look to government administrators for everything -- lobbying the mayor for garbage, the congressman for streets, a bigwig for contracts -- so that 'Nothing works without a lobby' and politicians spend, cheat and kill to win the power to dispense patronage.

He voices the frustration of those who risked their lives against the dictatorship: two and a half years after Marcos left, the people are still poor, government still inefficient, corruption still pervasive, because 'we merely had a change of leaders, not a change in values; a change of men, not a change in men.'

He charges that present government leaders enjoy 'the Marcosian habit of making themselves the ultimate source of all bounty and power,' and admits that his repeated pleas to civic clubs, religious groups and national leaders for honesty, hard work and self-discipline have 'fallen on deaf ears.'

He therefore brings the plea to the youth, asking them to denounce LUSOT, LAKAS and LAGAY and those who 'plunder the nation, corrupt our people and deprecate our values,' and to let their idealism and detachment from power and wealth be their strength.

He closes by challenging the NUSP -- which helped crush the dictatorship and fought colonialism -- to lead the crusade for 'a change, not just of men, but a change in men,' ending with the Tagalog battle cry 'Ibagsak ang LUSOT, LAKAS, at LAGAY. Ipugay ang KATAPATAN, KASIPAGAN at KATIMPIHAN.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 17 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the keynote address CJP gave on November 17, 1988 to the National Student Congress of the National Union of Students of the Philippines in Cebu City, 30 years after he founded the organization. He opened in recollection of his own student days -- his search for identity, singleminded pursuit of excellence and formation of enduring values -- when 'I was very poor; I had nothing' and was therefore truly free, having been elected FEU Central Student Organization president in 1957 as a second-year law student and then organizing the NUSP, and later the Institute of Student Affairs. He named three decades of NUSP leaders, restated its founding proposition that the best in man and society is attained 'only in freedom, dignity, equality and responsibility,' and congratulated the union for outgrowing purely student concerns to fight dictatorship, corruption and now poverty and oppression. Turning to the next 30 years, he posed one question: why, alone among the peoples of the Pacific, have the Filipinos remained poor? He rejected dictatorship as the answer, since Korea, Taiwan and Singapore had dictators too, 'without meaning to mitigate the guilt of the man in Hawaii'; rejected foreign exploitation, poor education and professional inferiority, since the Filipino excels abroad and 'is praised everywhere, except when he is in his own country.' His own answer was the 'godfather mentality' and the dole-out syndrome, which have made LAKAS, LUSOT and LAGAY -- influence, chicanery and bribery -- replace honest work, as in his favorite taxi driver's three-stage escape from every traffic violation. Twenty years of Marcosian dictatorship had trained people to look to government for everything, so that 'Nothing works without a lobby,' and 1986 had brought 'a change of leaders, not a change in values.' Having failed to move his elders, he brought the plea to the youth and challenged the NUSP to lead a crusade for honesty, hard work and self-discipline.
